The Benin Bronzes are several thousand brass and bronze plaques, heads and other sculptures made for the royal palace of the Kingdom of Benin, in what is now southern Nigeria. A royal guild of casters made them for the Oba, the king; the guild still works on Igun Street in Benin City. The casting tradition goes back to at least the 1300s.

  • Plaques: hundreds of rectangular panels that once covered the palace pillars, showing the Oba, chiefs, warriors, rituals and Portuguese traders. Most date from the 1500s and 1600s.
  • Heads: memorial heads of past kings and queen mothers, set on royal ancestral altars.
  • Other pieces: figures, bells and jewellery, alongside carved ivory such as the mask of Queen Mother Idia.

They were cast by the lost-wax method. Much of the metal came as brass bracelets (manillas) traded by Portuguese ships. Older West African casting includes the Igbo-Ukwu bronzes and the Ife heads.

In 1897 a British punitive expedition sacked Benin City and took the works away. Many were sold to pay its costs, and they spread to museums across Europe and America, with the largest group in the British Museum. Their skill upset European ideas about African art. Nigeria has asked for their return since independence. Since 2022 Germany and several other holders have handed ownership of many pieces back to Nigeria.
